name: Neo-Confucianism
summary: Neo-Confucianism is the Song-Ming revival of Confucian thought, systematised by Zhu Xi from the Northern Song masters and the Four Books, which grounds ethics in a cosmic principle (li) and makes self-cultivation the root of order. Its politics are moral: the state is ordered by the ruler's own virtue and example, beginning with the regulated family, and gain is not the state's prosperity. It opposes selfishness (si) in favour of public spirit (gong) and sought to restore China's Confucian culture; Zhu Xi even proposed a committee of moral experts to check imperial decisions.
scope: The Cheng-Zhu school (Cheng Yi, Cheng Hao, Zhu Xi) as the state-orthodox Neo-Confucianism (daoxue, lixue) of the Song through Qing dynasties, as the IEP and SEP present it: Zhu Xi's synthesis of Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai and the Cheng brothers, built on the Four Books (Great Learning, Analects, Mencius, Doctrine of the Mean) and the anthology Reflections on Things at Hand. Wang Yangming's mind-school (xinxue) is used only where it does not diverge from it. It is a moral philosophy with political implications, not a modern political programme; Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese variants and modern New Confucianism are not the basis.

keyFigures.role: Central synthesiser of Neo-Confucianism and compiler of the Four Books
keyFigures.quote: Zhu Xi’s thought has been the starting point for intellectual discourse and the focus of disputation for the last 800 years.

keyFigures.role: Northern Song master whose thought Zhu Xi synthesised
keyFigures.quote: Zhu fused the concepts of the principal Northern Song (960-1126 CE) thinkers, Shao Yong (1011-77), Zhou Dunyi (1017-73),  Zhang Zai (Chang Tsai, 1020-77) and the brothers Cheng Yi (1033-1107) and Cheng Hao (1032-85) into a rich, grand synthesis.

keyWorks.title: The Four Books

keyWorks.quote: The Four Books became required reading for the imperial examination system from the Yuan dynasty (1280-1341) until the system was abolished near the end of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) in 1908.

missingStatements.text: Rulers should be bound to cultivate their own virtue and set a moral example before they require it of the people.
missingStatements.rationale: The Great Learning, central to the Four Books, says the ruler must himself have the good qualities before requiring them of others, and ties ordering the state to cultivating the person.

missingStatements.text: Anyone, whatever their birth, can become a moral exemplar through sustained study and self-cultivation.
missingStatements.rationale: Zhu Xi held that anyone who sincerely commits to self-cultivation can make real progress toward sagehood, and aimed to open learning to all.
missingStatements.declined: Educational perfectibility is shared by many traditions and does not separate ideologies; not worth a permanent statement.

missingStatements.text: Funeral, wedding and ancestor rites should be observed according to a fixed ritual code.
missingStatements.rationale: Zhu Xi's Family Rituals gave detailed guidance for weddings, funerals and ancestor veneration, and li is described as the social glue that holds society together.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to Confucian ritual practice; too niche for the shared bank.

notes: Positions are recorded only where the IEP, the SEP and the Great Learning state them; economic, land, law and modern policy statements are null because those sources do not address them, and earlier answers resting on Wikipedia or on what the principles might imply were nulled. Themes searched in the saved texts: government and the ruler's example, family and filial duty, wealth and revenue, selfishness and public spirit, law and litigation, women and marriage, Buddhism and religion, examinations, foreign threats, tyrant removal. The Mencius, Doctrine of the Mean and Analects texts could not be fetched from classics.mit.edu or ctext.org, so the other three of the Four Books are not read. Wang Yangming's school diverges on authority and expertise.
